title: The Real Estate Brokerage War, For-Profit Education, & the Art of the Short with Brad Safalow
summary: Safalow favors Zillow over Compass, expects housing affordability to improve with lower rates, and argues that AI weakens Google advertising and education economics. He revisits shorts in Trupanion, Freshpet and Kinsale. Eisman explicitly shares selected education and pet-insurance concerns while disclosing Google ownership. Primary records confirm Washington listing restrictions, computing-enrollment declines and Kinsale premium softness, but challenge zero-growth pet insurance and simple Freshpet deterioration. Several private channel checks, liability accusations and valuation claims remain unresolved. The interview was recorded June 11, well before publication.
assessment: The episode offers differentiated mechanisms but many causal claims depend on private research. Keep Safalow stock calls separate from Eisman ownership and explicit endorsements. Subsequent operating results are mixed rather than uniform confirmation of the short theses.
speaker_map_notes: SPEAKER_01 is Eisman and SPEAKER_00 is Brad Safalow, established by the introduction and sustained question-answer roles. Embedded interviewer prompts are attributed by dialogue. Recording date June 11 is explicitly stated near 2110 seconds.
framework_points: Separate listing access from brokerage brand and lead generation.
Trace commission incidence and agent-broker splits.
Compare housing supply with household formation by region.
Distinguish price, revenue growth, dilution and cash generation.
Test insurance pricing with cohort aging and adverse selection.
Distinguish advertising claims from product safety.
Treat private research and management guidance as hypotheses requiring independent checks.
tools_and_charts: Broker commission splits and leverage multiples
Mortgage-rate buckets and household-adjusted housing turnover
State building permits and home-price changes
Zillow EBITDA, free cash flow, EPS and stock compensation
Enrollment by field, Pell share and graduate-loan exposure
Pet cohorts, churn, acquisition cost and premiums
Freshpet refrigerator placements and retail distribution
Insurance statutory closed-claim data and court searches
transcript_cautions: Published July 29 but explicitly recorded June 11, 2026.
Captions variously misspell Safalow, Reffkin, MLS and Homes.com.
The commission split is 80/20 from context; one caption renders 20/20.
Graduate PLUS and Parent PLUS wording is occasionally conflated; claims retain the graduate-financing context.
New Jersey is one of four large Trupanion states, not alone 40-45% of the business.
Closing summaries distinguish Eisman assertions from his reports of Safalow views.
